messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: School Counselor
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 43

She is 32, South Asian, married, and works as a school counselor, but when she first begins telling the story, she does not start with her job or even with her marriage. She starts with the day the shelling reaches the neighborhood where she lives. Until then, she thinks of the war as something that happens in other parts of the city, something carried in on the radio, in rumors, in the tense faces of neighbors at the market. She keeps going to work at the school, trying to be steady for the children, telling herself that routines still matter. She is the kind of person who checks on others before she checks on herself. Even then, she notices how often she is listening for distant booms, how she keeps her shoes near the bed, how she scans the street before stepping outside.

The day everything changes begins like many others. She is at work when the first blast comes close enough to shake the windows. The children freeze. A teacher yells for everyone to get down. She remembers the sound more than the sight at first: the crack of something breaking apart, the sudden silence after, then shouting. She moves on instinct, gathering younger children into a corridor away from the windows. She counts heads again and again, because counting gives her something concrete to hold onto when everything feels unreal. When she finally reaches her husband later that evening, she cannot stop shaking. He tries to reassure her, but she keeps asking where the next strike will fall, how they will know when to leave, whether they should leave at all.

After that day, the world becomes organized around danger. She sleeps in fragments, waking at every noise, and by morning she feels as though she has already worked a full day before getting out of bed. She begins having images that arrive without warning: the children crouched under desks, dust drifting through the classroom, a little girl crying for her mother. These pictures come to her while she is making tea, while she is speaking to a parent, while she is trying to write notes for students who need support. At school, she becomes even more careful than before, but now her vigilance has a cost. She sits near the door. She notices exit routes. She startles when someone drops a book. Her body seems to live ahead of her, always braced.

The work that once gave her purpose begins to feel heavier. As a counselor, she is expected to stay calm for frightened students, many of whom are dealing with displacement, loss, and constant uncertainty. She listens to children talk about missing fathers, about nights spent in basements, about the way their mothers cry quietly when they think no one hears. She does what she can, but afterward she goes home carrying all of it with her. She finds herself going numb during conversations, as if some part of her has stepped back to watch from a distance. At times she is not sure she is fully in the room, even with her husband sitting across from her. He says she is there but not there. She hears him, but the words feel far away.

She avoids anything that reminds her too directly of that day. She turns off the news quickly. She refuses to walk past the schoolyard when she hears construction noise that resembles gunfire. She stops meeting neighbors as often because talk about the war makes her stomach clench. Yet she cannot avoid reminders entirely, and when they find her, they hit hard. The smell of smoke from a generator sends her into panic before she can think. A child slamming a locker door makes her heart race. Once, when a loud truck passes outside her apartment, she drops to the floor before she realizes what she is doing. Afterwards she feels embarrassed, then angry at herself for being unable to control her own body.

At home, she and her husband move carefully around each other. He wants to comfort her, but she becomes irritable when he asks how she is sleeping or whether she has eaten. She knows she is short-tempered, knows she snaps over small things, and then feels guilty almost immediately. Some evenings she sits awake long after he has gone to bed, staring at the dark window and thinking about how quickly ordinary life can disappear. She misses the version of herself who believed that if she worked hard and stayed organized, she could keep people safe. Now she understands how fragile that belief was, and that loss sits in her like grief.

Still, she continues to go to the school. She continues to sit with children who are afraid, and she speaks to them in a voice she is trying to reclaim for herself. On her better days, she notices moments of warmth—a student drawing a picture, her husband leaving tea beside her chair, the brief quiet before the morning bell. Even then, she remains alert, carrying the war inside her body as if it might return at any moment.
